title: The Superiority of the Son over Angels
english: … for human nature ranks below the glory of the angels, yet even so he was “far above every name that is named” (Ephesians 1:21).

On Hebrews 1:7–8: With “radiance” and “stamp” he followed John’s thought, for John called him the Word and said that he was with God. Here too he follows John. John said, “He was in the beginning” (John 1:2) and “All things came into being through him” (John 1:3), meaning: he was, and these things were not. So too Paul: to the angels, “who makes”, but to the Son, “your throne”. He wants to show that what is made once was not, while the one whose throne is eternal was always with the Father.

On Hebrews 1:12–14: He is not speaking of a change in their nature but making a comparison. These things are more liable to perish, and set beside the everlasting life of the Son they are as good as perishing. Indeed, the Lord, foretelling his second coming, says that the stars will fall (Matthew 24:29), but no longer the sun, the moon or the heaven. “To which of the angels has he ever said …?” Passing over the whole creation, he names what stands above it, the angels. For if the Son differs from the angels, in that they came into being and he did not, how much more does he differ from all the invisible things? Notice also that by saying “But you are the same”, he showed that the Son’s nature is before the ages and cannot change. And by saying “Are they not all ministering spirits sent to serve?”, he showed that the Son is not a minister but a fellow worker.

On Hebrews 2:2–3: He does not mean the law, but the word that was many times delivered through angels. “It was confirmed to us by those who heard.” This is like the passage in the letter to the Galatians: “I went up by revelation and laid before them the gospel, lest somehow I should be running, or had run, in vain” (Galatians 2:2). It was confirmed, not because we needed it, but so that all the others might be fully assured that what I preach, I preach rightly.

On Hebrews 2:5–9: He means the age to come. And straight after, at the end, he added: “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him; but we see Jesus, made a little lower than the angels” (Hebrews 2:8–9). So the words “What is man, that you remember him?” (Hebrews 2:6), he says, belong to Jesus, since what belongs to our common humanity belonged to him. But it is the Son himself who says, “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise because of your enemies” (Psalm 8:2) and “I will look at the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Psalm 8:3). No one would say that the man whom God remembered is the one who did this, the one who “prepared praise out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies because of your enemies” and who will “look at the heavens, the works of your fingers”. It is the Son who remembered the man and made him a little lower than the angels. And who is the man? Jesus. Because of the suffering of death he was made a little lower than the …

title: The Superiority of the Melchizedekian Priesthood
english: … angels.
On Hebrews 3:13: He presents the present age as a single day.
On Hebrews 4:12: He speaks of a dividing of soul and spirit when the soul is drawn to share what the body feels, while the grace of the Holy Spirit pulls the other way, toward heavenly things.

On Hebrews 6:1–2: Christ’s beginning was in Judaism, for he lived according to the law. That is why he says: let us leave this behind and press on to perfection, knowing that the one who was to be a priest without the law had to be after the order of Melchizedek. “From dead works, and of faith toward God, of baptisms”: for Christians, earthly things are dead. So it is absurd, he says, for people who have left this way of life, whether we call it the life of faith or the life of those who have died to everything, to go back again to the washings of the law. When the Lord came, he preached repentance, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near” (Matthew 4:17); and that repentance is repentance from dead works. So the phrase should be read like this: “of repentance from dead works”, meaning “of the repentance that turns from dead works”. What he means, then, is this: we must not abandon repentance from dead works, faith in God and baptism and run back to the law. He named baptism in the plural because of the great number of those found worthy of it; and he spoke of the teaching about baptisms, the laying on of hands, by which ordinations are made, the hope of the resurrection and the rest. He is preparing the ground for what follows: the priests under the law upheld the law, but Melchizedek stood outside the law, and the one who came was after the order of Melchizedek. We must not, he says, abandon the priest after the order of Melchizedek and take up the cause of the priesthood under the law, as if to keep the things of the law standing. He called the things of the law a “foundation” because they were, for human beings, the prelude to godliness.

On Hebrews 6:5–6: The apostles raised the dead, and that was the power of the resurrection. He said “holding him up to contempt” because, if baptism is a mystery, once is enough. If the act is repeated, it becomes contempt and public shame.

On Hebrews 6:7–8: He took this illustration not with baptism in view (how could it be, when he was ruling out a second baptism?) but for the power of the Holy Spirit, which does us good again and again.

On Hebrews 6:17: Having spoken earlier of “the full assurance of hope” (Hebrews 6:11), he showed that God gave Abraham full assurance, not the kind that comes through works and belongs to one’s way of life, but the kind that comes through God’s own dispensation. Once God had sworn, he could not change; the power of the promise could not be altered.

On Hebrews 7:1–2: He does not mention for nothing how Melchizedek met Abraham after his victory over the Assyrians, and how Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. He means to show that the forefather of the tribe of Levi had Melchizedek for his priest. So the priesthood without the law is greater than the priesthood …

title: Melchizedek and the Law
english: … under the law.

On Hebrews 7:3: “Without father, without mother, without genealogy” refers to the priesthood. In the tribe of Levi it was plain whose son each man was: which priest was his father and which priestly woman his mother. There were also set terms of priesthood: some priests served yearly courses of duty, others served as priests for their whole lives. Both kinds are found among the priests under the law, though not in the same periods. He calls Melchizedek fatherless, motherless and without genealogy, with neither beginning of days nor end of life, as far as the priesthood is concerned. He had no priestly family. He did not begin at some point as the successor of another, nor take over from another at the change of a course, nor did he have a law that made him priest for life. In short, everything said of him is said by comparison with the priests under the law. It is said of Melchizedek: “made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever.” How, then, does Melchizedek remain a priest? The statement raises a question, and this is the answer. Just as the law is called “Moses”, so here “Melchizedek” sometimes means the man and sometimes the priesthood itself. If, then, Melchizedek has been made like the Son through the priesthood that is according to Christ, he remains for ever: not the man, for he was mortal, but the dignity of the priesthood.
On Hebrews 9:11: The tent was built in Moses’ time so that worship could be offered in it. This tent is greater: it is the establishment of grace, the body of Christ, which has Christ for its head.
On Hebrews 11:20: “By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come.” He put Jacob first and Esau second, not in the order of their birth, but in the order of the blessing.

On Hebrews 11:38: “Of whom the world was not worthy.” He does not say this of everyone, but of the last group, whom he also knows as martyrs. He also mentions those who “turned back armies” (Hebrews 11:34) and who received grace for the good of the people.

On Hebrews 12:1: “Laying aside every weight.” The weight is the sin of fleshly pleasure, and from it is born the sin that so easily besets us. He calls sin “easily besetting” because it readily surrounds us and draws us into doing its will.
On Hebrews 12:22–23: The glory given to God is the festal gathering and feast of the angels; “and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all.”
On Hebrews 12:27: This is what Paul says elsewhere: “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:31). The temporary must pass, so that the eternal may come.
On Hebrews 13:10–13: That is, those under the law do not have this gift in which we share. “Outside the camp” means outside the ordinances of the law and the camp of Israel.
